title: Future participles and fact clauses
intro: This unit completes the participles and adds fact clauses. `-jAk` describes what is going to happen (*okajak kitabym*, the book I'm going to read), `-mAdYk` what hasn't happened (*okamadyk kitabym*, a book I haven't read). With `-dYgY`, a whole clause becomes the object of *bilmek*, *eşitmek* or *aýtmak*: *Onuň gelendigini bilýärin*, I know (that) he has come. Last comes the doer inside a clause, in the genitive: *Aýnanyň okan kitaby*, the book Aýna read.

sections.title: -jAk: the book I'm going to read

blocks.text: You know `-jAk` as the future: *Men ertir okajak* ([A2 unit 3](a2-u03)). The same form stands before a noun for what is going to happen: *geljek myhmanlar* (the guests who are coming), *okajak kitabym* (the book I'm going to read), *gitjek ýerimiz* (the place we're going to). It works exactly like `-ýAn` and `-An` in [B1 unit 5](b1-u05): when the noun is the thing done, its possessive ending says who will do it.

blocks.label: -jAk before a noun
lines: geljek myhmanlar  guests who will come
okajak kitabym    the book I'll read
gelmejek adam     one who won't come

blocks.text: **Alone, with an ending.** Used as a noun, `-jAk` takes the possessive endings itself, and its k becomes g before a vowel: *aýtjagym* (what I'm going to say). *Aýtjagymy ýatdan çykardym*, I've forgotten what I was going to say.

items.en: The guests who are coming are from Mary.
This is the book I'm going to read.
The place we're going to isn't far.
Is there anyone who won't come to the wedding?
I've forgotten what I was going to say.

blocks.title: You already use it
blocks.text: *Geljek hepde* (next week) and *geljek ýyl* (next year) are this participle: the week, the year that is to come. The t of *gitmek* stays before *-jek*, as in the future: *gitjek ýerimiz*.

`-mAdYk` is the negative of `-An`: what has not happened, or did not happen. *Okamadyk kitabym* (a book I haven't read), *görmedik ýerim* (a place I've never seen), *tanamadyk adam* (someone you don't know, a stranger). Like `-An`, it can also describe the doer: *gelmedik myhmanlar* (the guests who didn't come).

blocks.label: Forms
lines: k → g before a vowel: okamadygym

blocks.caption: Three negatives before a noun
head: Turkmen
English
rows: the guests who aren't coming, who don't come

items.en: This is a book I haven't read.
There are many places in Turkmenistan I haven't seen.
There's a man I don't know at the door.
I called the guests who didn't come.
There's a film we haven't seen yet.

blocks.title: Not the future
blocks.text: *Okamadyk kitabym* is a book I **haven't** read; *okamajak kitabym* is a book I **won't** read.

sections.title: Fact clauses: -dYgY after bilmek, eşitmek, aýtmak

blocks.text: English joins a fact to **know**, **hear** or **say** with **that**: **I know that he has come**. Turkmen has no such word. It turns the clause into a noun with `-dYgY` and makes that noun the object: *Onuň gelendigini bilýärin*. Build it from a participle: `-An` + `-dYk` (k → g) + the possessive of the doer + the accusative.
**The tense is in the participle.** `-An` for what happened, `-ýAn` for what is going on or usual, `-jAk` for what will happen:

blocks.caption: Three tenses
head: Turkmen
English
rows: I know he's coming. I know he comes.

blocks.text: **The person** is the possessive ending, and the genitive pronoun is optional, as in *(meniň) gitmegim* ([B1 unit 4](b1-u04)): *(meniň) gelendigimi*, *(seniň) gelendigiňi*. When the doer is the same person as the subject of the main verb, the pronoun is left out: *Merjen ertir geljekdigini aýtdy*, Merjen said she would come tomorrow.

blocks.title: *gelmek*: that I came, that you came…

items.en: I know she works in Ashgabat.
I heard you got married!
Merjen said she would come tomorrow.
I didn't know they had moved to Mary.
We heard you're coming.
I don't believe he has come.
items.note: *Ynanmak* takes the dative, so the clause does too: *gelendigine*.

blocks.text: **Nouns and adjectives** take `-dYgY` straight on, for **is**: *onuň mugallymdygyny* (that she is a teacher), *howanyň sowukdygyny* (that it's cold), *pulumyň ýokdugyny* (that I have no money). Its vowel follows the rounding rule: *ýokdugyny*. The negative is *däl*: *ýadaw däldigini* (that he isn't tired).

items.en: I know she's a teacher.
I heard it's cold.
My dad doesn't know I have no money.
He said he wasn't tired.

blocks.text: **Questions inside.** The same form carries **where**, **when**, **who** and **what**: *Onuň nirede işleýändigini bilýärsiňmi?* (do you know where he works?), *Haçan geljekdigini aýtmady* (he didn't say when he would come).

items.en: Do you know where he works?
Merdan didn't say when he'd come.
I don't know who came.
Do you know where the book is?

blocks.title: Keep the person and the case
blocks.text: The ending says who: *meniň gelendigimi* (that I came), *onuň gelendigini* (that he came). The doer goes in the genitive: *onuň gelendigini*, not `ol gelendigini`. And after *bilmek*, *eşitmek*, *aýtmak* the clause needs the accusative: *gelendigini bilýärin*, not `gelendigi bilýärin`.

blocks.title: A shorter form you'll see
blocks.text: With `-jAk`, a form without *-dYk* is also common: *gitjegini aýtdy* (he said he'd go). This course writes *gitjekdigini*; recognize both.

sections.title: The doer inside: Aýnanyň okan kitaby

blocks.text: In [B1 unit 5](b1-u05) the doer of a participle was a pronoun: *(meniň) okan kitabym*. When the doer is a noun, it goes in the **genitive**, and the noun at the end takes **its**, `-(s)Y`: *Aýnanyň okan kitaby*, the book Aýna read; *kakamyň işleýän ýeri*, the place where my father works; *mugallymyň beren kitaby*, the book the teacher gave.

blocks.caption: Who did it
head: Doer
Turkmen
English
rows: the place where my father works
the place where the children play

blocks.text: **Genitive or not?** Look at the noun at the end. If it is the **doer**, nothing goes in the genitive and the noun has no possessive: *kitaby okan gyz* (the girl who read the book). If it is the **thing done**, a place or a time, the doer goes in the genitive and the noun gets the matching possessive: *gyzyň okan kitaby* (the book the girl read). With a pronoun the genitive word can be dropped, since the ending says who: *okan kitabym*. With a noun, keep it: *Aýnanyň okan kitaby*.

items.tk: Aýnanyň maslahat beren filmi gaty gyzykly.
items.seg: Aýna|nyň maslahat ber|en film|i gaty gyzykly.
items.en: The film Aýna recommended is really interesting.

items.tk: Kakamyň işleýän ýeri şu ýerden uzak däl.
items.seg: Kaka|m|yň işle|ýän ýer|i şu ýer|den uzak däl.
items.en: The place where my father works isn't far from here.
Have you read the book the teacher gave?
The place where the children play is in the garden.
The girl who read the book is my little sister.

lines.en: How was the book you read last week?

lines.tk: Örän gyzykly! Ony maňa Aýna maslahat berdi. Aýnanyň maslahat beren kitaplary hemişe gowy.
lines.en: Really interesting! Aýna recommended it to me. The books Aýna has recommended are always good.
Don't tell me what happens at the end!

lines.tk: Bolýar, aýtmaryn. Seniň ony okamagyňy isleýärin.
lines.en: OK, I won't. I want you to read it.
Then I'll get the book from you tomorrow.

blocks.title: Two endings, both needed
blocks.text: *Aýnanyň okan kitaby*: the genitive on the doer and **its** on the noun. Not `Aýnanyň okan kitap`, with no possessive. And when the noun is the doer, neither: *kitaby okan gyz*, not `kitabyň okan gyzy`.

summary: `-jAk` before a noun: what will happen (*geljek myhmanlar*, *okajak kitabym*); negative `-mAjAk` (*gelmejek adam*). Alone it takes endings with k → g: *aýtjagym*.
`-mAdYk` is the negative of `-An`: *okamadyk kitabym*, *görmedik ýerim*, *gelmedik myhmanlar*.
Fact clauses: participle + `-dYk` + possessive + case, as the object of *bilmek*, *eşitmek*, *aýtmak*: *Onuň gelendigini bilýärin*.
The participle carries the tense (*gelendigini, gelýändigini, geljekdigini*); nouns and adjectives take `-dYgY` directly (*mugallymdygyny, ýokdugyny, däldigini*).
Question words fit inside: *Onuň nirede işleýändigini bilýärsiňmi?*
A noun doer goes in the genitive and the noun at the end takes its possessive: *Aýnanyň okan kitaby*, *kakamyň işleýän ýeri*; when the noun is the doer, neither: *kitaby okan gyz*.
